claim: Morphogen signaling contributes to the patterned spatiotemporal expression of genes during development.
source: Morphogen signaling contributes to the patterned spatiotemporal expression of genes during development.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus about morphogen function.

claim: One mode of regulation of signaling-responsive genes is at the level of transcription.
source: One mode of regulation of signaling-responsive genes is at the level of transcription.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about gene regulation mechanisms.

claim: Transcription occurs intermittently, in bursts.
source: Single-cell quantitative studies of transcription have revealed that transcription occurs intermittently, in bursts.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on transcriptional bursting.

claim: The transcription levels of genes downstream of Wg and Dpp morphogen gradients appear to share a common method of control via burst frequency modulation.
source: We compared our experimental results with predictions from stochastic models of transcription, which indicated that the transcription levels of these genes appear to share a common method of control via burst frequency modulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on comparison of experimental data with computational models.

claim: Morphogens form spatially-extended gradients from the source of their synthesis.
source: Morphogens form spatially-extended gradients from the source of their synthesis, and elicit different transcription outputs from target genes, depending on local concentration of the morphogen (Tabata and Takei, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Morphogens elicit different transcription outputs from target genes, depending on local concentration of the morphogen.
source: Morphogens form spatially-extended gradients from the source of their synthesis, and elicit different transcription outputs from target genes, depending on local concentration of the morphogen (Tabata and Takei, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Many paracrine signals regulate gene transcription via control of the availability or activity of sequence-specific transcription factors.
source: Many paracrine signals regulate gene transcription via control of the availability or activity of sequence-specific transcription factors.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about paracrine signaling mechanisms.

claim: Some transcription factors regulate assembly of the preinitiation complex composed of Pol II and general factors at the transcription start site.
source: Some transcription factors regulate assembly of the preinitiation complex composed of Pol II and general factors at the transcription start site (Esnault et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Other factors recruit coregulators that modify nucleosomes or remodel the chromatin architecture of the gene.
source: Other factors recruit coregulators that modify nucleosomes or remodel the chromatin architecture of the gene (Bannister and Kouzarides, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Genes that are constitutively expressed rarely show uniform and continuous mRNA synthesis.
source: Genes that are constitutively expressed rarely show uniform and continuous mRNA synthesis.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about transcriptional dynamics.

claim: mRNA synthesis occurs in bursts that are interrupted by periods of dormant output.
source: Rather, mRNA synthesis occurs in bursts that are interrupted by periods of dormant output. This phenomenon is known as transcriptional bursting (Chen et al., 2019; Chubb et al., 2006; Dey et al., 2015; Raj et al., 2006; Suter et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work on transcriptional bursting.

claim: The availability of transcription factors has been shown to affect burst frequency.
source: The availability of transcription factors has been shown to affect burst frequency (Ezer et al., 2016; Larson et al., 2013; Senecal et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Drosophila transcription factors Bicoid and Dorsal have been studied in great detail with respect to their effects on transcription burst frequency in the embryo.
source: For example, the Drosophila transcription factors Bicoid and Dorsal have been studied in great detail with respect to their effects on transcription burst frequency in the embryo (Garcia et al., 2013; He et al., 2012; Holloway and Spirov, 2017; Little et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Enhancer strength and enhancer-promoter contact correlate with burst frequency of genes.
source: Enhancer strength and enhancer-promoter contact correlate with burst frequency of genes (Bartman et al., 2016; Bothma et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2019; Fukaya et al., 2016; Larsson et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Bursting frequency is potentiated by enhancer-promoter contact and is mediated by transcription factors binding to DNA.
source: These studies altogether suggest that bursting frequency is potentiated by enhancer-promoter contact and is mediated by transcription factors binding to DNA.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple cited studies.

claim: Wg is produced in cells at the boundary between Dorsal and Ventral (DV) compartments of the wing pouch.
source: Wg is produced in cells at the boundary between Dorsal and Ventral (DV) compartments of the wing pouch, while Dpp is produced in cells at the boundary between Anterior and Posterior (AP) compartments (Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 1A and reflects established knowledge about wing disc morphogen expression.

claim: Dpp is produced in cells at the boundary between Anterior and Posterior (AP) compartments.
source: Wg is produced in cells at the boundary between Dorsal and Ventral (DV) compartments of the wing pouch, while Dpp is produced in cells at the boundary between Anterior and Posterior (AP) compartments (Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 1A and reflects established knowledge about wing disc morphogen expression.

claim: Dpp regulates gene expression in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: These factors form concentration gradients across the disc, and in the case of Dpp, it regulates gene expression in a concentration-dependent manner.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about Dpp function.

claim: Sens is expressed in two stripes of cells adjacent to and on either side of the DV boundary in the wing pouch.
source: Sens is required for cells to adopt a sensory organ fate, and the gene is expressed in two stripes of cells adjacent to and on either side of the DV boundary in the wing pouch (Figure 1B,C; Nolo et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to figures and a citation to prior work.

claim: Sens expression in the wing pouch is induced by Wg, which is expressed by cells located at the DV boundary.
source: Sens expression in the wing pouch is induced by Wg, which is expressed by cells located at the DV boundary (Jafar-Nejad et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The genomic transgene rescues the endogenous gene based on function and expression.
source: First, the genomic transgene rescues the endogenous gene based on function and expression (Cassidy et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The fluorescence signal was specific for sfGFP-sens since wing discs from larvae not carrying the transgene gave a low background fluorescence pattern.
source: The fluorescence signal was specific for sfGFP-sens since wing discs from larvae not carrying the transgene gave a low background fluorescence pattern (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The size of each 2D spot was approximately the expected diffraction limit of ~600 nm for smFISH probes emitting at 633 nm wavelength.
source: The size of each 2D spot was approximately the expected diffraction limit of ~600 nm for smFISH probes emitting at 633 nm wavelength (Lipson et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and reflects physical principles of microscopy.

claim: The distribution of fluorescence intensity for the identified 3D spots was unimodal, suggesting that the spots had a homogeneous composition.
source: The distribution of fluorescence intensity for the identified 3D spots was unimodal, suggesting that the spots had a homogeneous composition (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Incubation of wing discs in medium containing actinomycin-D greatly diminished the number of fluorescence spots.
source: Second, we incubated wing discs in medium containing actinomycin-D, an inhibitor of mRNA synthesis. The number of fluorescence spots was greatly diminished, as would be expected if they were localized to mRNA molecules (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: 0.5% of identified spots are false-positive.
source: From this, we estimated that 0.5% of identified spots are false-positive (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate based on experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: A maximum of 6% of mRNAs (232 out of 3842 spots scored) were not identified by both probe-sets.
source: The analysis indicated that a maximum of 6% of mRNAs (232 out of 3842 spots scored) were not identified by both probe-sets (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result based on experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: This rate of false-negative identification is comparable to smFISH methods in other systems.
source: This rate of false-negative identification is comparable to smFISH methods in other systems (Raj et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The abundance of sens mRNAs within the DV stripes varied from one to fifty molecules per cell.
source: The abundance of sens mRNAs within the DV stripes varied from one to fifty molecules per cell (Figure 1F), reflecting the graded expression pattern of Sens protein induced by the Wg morphogen across the width of each stripe (Jafar-Nejad et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a quantitative result based on experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The abundance of sens mRNAs reflects the graded expression pattern of Sens protein induced by the Wg morphogen across the width of each stripe.
source: The abundance of sens mRNAs within the DV stripes varied from one to fifty molecules per cell (Figure 1F), reflecting the graded expression pattern of Sens protein induced by the Wg morphogen across the width of each stripe (Jafar-Nejad et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and supported by a citation.

claim: Peaks in mRNA number per cell were observed as a function of distance from the DV boundary.
source: Binning cells according to their distance from the DV boundary, we were able to observe peaks in mRNA number per cell as a function of distance from the boundary (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a result based on experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: sens is expressed in a stripe of cells located within the morphogenetic furrow in the eye disc.
source: In the eye disc, sens is expressed in a stripe of cells located within the morphogenetic furrow, and indeed we were able to detect smFISH signals in furrow cells of the eye disc (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The smFISH method is broadly applicable to imaginal discs.
source: Thus, our method is broadly applicable to imaginal discs.
evidence: This is an inference based on successful application of the method to multiple disc types.

claim: Salm is symmetrically expressed in a domain somewhat broader than the Dpp stripe.
source: Salm is symmetrically expressed in a domain somewhat broader than the Dpp stripe, whereas omb and dad are expressed more broadly, and brk is expressed only near the wing pouch border (de Celis et al., 1996; Grimm and Pflugfelder, 1996; Tabata and Takei, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: omb and dad are expressed more broadly than salm.
source: Salm is symmetrically expressed in a domain somewhat broader than the Dpp stripe, whereas omb and dad are expressed more broadly, and brk is expressed only near the wing pouch border (de Celis et al., 1996; Grimm and Pflugfelder, 1996; Tabata and Takei, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: brk is expressed only near the wing pouch border.
source: Salm is symmetrically expressed in a domain somewhat broader than the Dpp stripe, whereas omb and dad are expressed more broadly, and brk is expressed only near the wing pouch border (de Celis et al., 1996; Grimm and Pflugfelder, 1996; Tabata and Takei, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: smFISH qualitatively recapitulated the known expression patterns of salm, omb, dad, and brk genes.
source: When smFISH was used to detect mRNAs of these genes, it qualitatively recapitulated their known expression patterns (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The distributions in mRNA number per cell displayed profiles that were consistent with previous qualitative descriptions of their expression patterns.
source: When we did so, the distributions in mRNA number per cell displayed profiles that were consistent with previous qualitative descriptions of their expression patterns (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The sd gene is expressed uniformly throughout the wing pouch.
source: To ensure that these distributions were not an artifact of landmarking the border, we probed for mRNAs produced from the scalloped (sd) gene. The sd gene is expressed uniformly throughout the wing pouch (Campbell et al., 1992; Williams et al., 1993), and thus we anticipated a uniform distribution of mRNAs/cell if our method was accurate.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There was a fairly constant level of sd mRNAs/cell across the wing pouch as determined by the smFISH pipeline.
source: Indeed, there was a fairly constant level of mRNAs/cell across the wing pouch as determined by our smFISH pipeline (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Quantification of pixel intensity of all fluorescent spots revealed two discrete populations: a large population of dim spots of uniform intensity, and a smaller population of brighter spots with more variable intensity.
source: Quantification of pixel intensity of all fluorescent spots revealed two discrete populations: a large population of dim spots of uniform intensity, and a smaller population of brighter spots with more variable intensity (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is a result based on experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The dim spots correspond to mature mRNAs located primarily in the cytoplasm.
source: The former population corresponded to those described earlier, and they were primarily located in the cytoplasm - these are the mature mRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization of the spots.

claim: The brighter spots correspond to sites of nascent transcription located primarily inside nuclei.
source: The latter population was primarily located inside nuclei, and thus we hypothesized that these were sites of nascent transcription.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the localization of the spots.

claim: Probes complementary to an intron in the omb gene only detected the brighter population of spots localized to nuclei.
source: To confirm that these bright spots corresponded to transcription sites, we used probes complementary to an intron in the omb gene. These probes only detected the brighter population of spots localized to nuclei (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Introns are not spliced out until after transcription.
source: Since introns are not spliced out until after transcription, this result supports the conclusion that the brighter nuclear spots are sites of nascent transcription.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about RNA processing.

claim: The brighter nuclear spots are sites of nascent transcription.
source: Since introns are not spliced out until after transcription, this result supports the conclusion that the brighter nuclear spots are sites of nascent transcription.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data and established knowledge.

claim: Fewer than 15% of nuclei contained more than one transcription site for a given gene.
source: Although wing disc cells are diploid, fewer than 15% of nuclei contained more than one transcription site for a given gene.
evidence: This is a quantitative result based on experimental observations.

claim: Drosophila and other animals have extensive physical pairing of homologous chromosomes in somatic cells.
source: Drosophila and other animals have extensive physical pairing of homologous chromosomes in somatic cells (McKee, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Alleles on paired chromosomes are often spatially juxtaposed.
source: Consequently, alleles on paired chromosomes are often spatially juxtaposed (Szabo et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Between 50–80% of all cells had mature mRNAs but did not have a detectable transcription site.
source: Strikingly, many cells did not have a detectable transcription site even though the cells contained mature mRNAs (Figure 3E). Between 50–80% of all cells had this feature, and it was observed for all genes.
evidence: This is a quantitative result based on experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The observation that many cells lack transcription sites is not an artifact of segmentation erroneously assigning mature mRNAs to cells that do not express the genes.
source: This observation is not an artifact of segmentation erroneously assigning mature mRNAs to cells that do not express the genes. For all genes, the number of transcription sites strongly correlated with mRNA number when discs were binned but not segmented (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The ratio of variance to mean mature mRNA number per cell was between 5 and 10 for all genes.
source: The ratio of variance to mean mature mRNA number per cell was between 5 and 10 for all genes, and was fairly independent of mRNA output (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result based on experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A Poisson process could not explain why transcription sites were not detected in every cell expressing mRNA.
source: This indicated that a Poisson process could not explain why we failed to detect transcription sites in every cell expressing mRNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the variance-to-mean ratio data.

claim: The transcription elongation rate is assumed to be 1100 nucleotides/min, which is a value that has been experimentally determined in Drosophila.
source: The model also includes a transcription elongation step, which is assumed to be 100% processive, and whose timescale depends on the gene length and the rate of elongation. The latter is assumed to be 1100 nucleotides/min, which is a value that has been experimentally determined in Drosophila (Ardehali et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A broad range of burst size and frequency could explain the observed frequency of finding cells with a transcription site.
source: We then asked what combination of burst size and frequency could theoretically account for the observed frequency of finding cells with a transcription site (this ranged from 20% to 50% of cells). A phase diagram revealed that a broad range of burst size and frequency could explain our experimental observations (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Tuning burst frequency and/or size can produce the variable likelihood of detecting a transcription site by smFISH.
source: Therefore, according to our model results, tuning burst frequency and/or size can produce the variable likelihood of detecting a transcription site by smFISH.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on computational modeling results.

claim: The frequency of detecting a transcription site varied across the disc in a manner that was gene-specific.
source: We quantified the frequency of detecting a transcription site as a function of cell position within the wing pouch (Figure 5A,B). This frequency varied across the disc in a manner that was gene-specific.
evidence: This is a result based on experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The spatial distributions of transcription site frequency strongly paralleled the mRNA number per cell for all genes.
source: Strikingly, the spatial distributions of transcription site frequency strongly paralleled the mRNA number per cell for all genes (compare Figure 5A,B and Figures 1G and 2H).
evidence: This is a result based on comparison of experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The frequency of detecting a transcription site for sd was constant across the disc and paralleled the sd mRNA number per cell.
source: To ensure that this was not an artifact of variable smFISH detection, we also quantified the frequency of detecting a transcription site for sd, which is uniformly expressed in the wing pouch. This frequency was constant across the disc and paralleled the sd mRNA number per cell (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Average mRNA number per cell and the likelihood of detecting a transcription site were linearly correlated with one another for all genes.
source: We further examined the relationship between mRNA number per cell and transcription site frequency (Figure 5C,D). Average mRNA number per cell and the likelihood of detecting a transcription site were linearly correlated with one another for all genes.
evidence: This is a result based on experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The positive correlation confirms that Dpp and Wg regulate gene expression primarily through control of transcription initiation.
source: The positive correlation confirms that Dpp and Wg regulate gene expression primarily through control of transcription initiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlation.

claim: The slopes of linear fits for three Dpp-responsive genes, brk, omb, and salm, were not significantly different from one another.
source: Remarkably, the slopes of linear fits for three Dpp-responsive genes, brk, omb, and salm, were not significantly different from one another, and the slope for dad was similar to brk and omb but smaller than for salm (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a result based on statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The conserved linear relationship between gene transcription and mRNA number suggests that mRNA decay rates are not very different between these Dpp target genes.
source: This conserved linear relationship between gene transcription and mRNA number has several implications. It suggests that mRNA decay rates are not very different between these Dpp target genes since the slopes would be different from one another if decay rates varied.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed linear relationship.

claim: mRNA decay is not being actively regulated by Dpp.
source: Moreover, since the slopes are constant over a broad range of mRNA output, it suggests that mRNA decay is not being actively regulated by Dpp.
evidence: This is an inference based on the constant slopes observed.

claim: The average number of nascent RNAs per transcription site did not significantly vary between cells that were receiving different levels of Dpp and Wg signal.
source: We sought to determine whether burst size or frequency was being regulated. We did so by estimating the number of nascent RNAs at each transcription site, which was quantified as a multiple of the median pixel intensity of mature RNA spots (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The average number of nascent RNAs per transcription site did not significantly vary between cells that were receiving different levels of Dpp and Wg signal (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is a result based on experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The average number of nascent RNAs per transcription site was independent of the likelihood that transcription was occurring in a cell.
source: Moreover, the average number of nascent RNAs per transcription site was also independent of the likelihood that transcription was occurring in a cell (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a result based on experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The propensity for a cell to generate nascent transcripts does not correlate with the number of nascent transcripts.
source: Therefore, the propensity for a cell to generate nascent transcripts does not correlate with the number of nascent transcripts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: When burst size is modulated, there is a positive correlation between nascent RNA number in a transcription site and the probability of detecting a transcription site.
source: We first considered whether modulation of transcription burst size by Wg and Dpp could explain our observations. We modulated burst size by systematically varying the kini parameter, and from simulations, then calculated the number of nascent RNAs per transcription site and the transcription site detection frequency. There was a positive correlation between nascent RNA number in a transcription site and the probability of detecting a transcription site (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Model predictions for burst size modulation were not observed in the experimental results with the target genes.
source: None of these model predictions were observed in the experimental results with the target genes (Figure 6C). It suggests that transcription burst size is not strongly regulated by Dpp and Wg.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of model predictions with experimental data.

claim: Transcription burst size is not strongly regulated by Dpp and Wg.
source: None of these model predictions were observed in the experimental results with the target genes (Figure 6C). It suggests that transcription burst size is not strongly regulated by Dpp and Wg.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of model predictions with experimental data.

claim: When burst frequency is modulated, there is little change in nascent RNA number as transcription site frequency changes.
source: We then modulated burst frequency in the model by systematically varying kon, and calculated the number of nascent RNAs per transcription site and the transcription site frequency. There was little change in nascent RNA number as transcription site frequency changed, even across a wide range of fixed burst sizes (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in the referenced figures.

claim: All model predictions for burst frequency modulation agree well with the experimental results.
source: All of these model predictions agree well with the experimental results (Figure 6C). This suggests that Dpp and Wg regulation of genes in the wing disc primarily occurs by modulation of transcriptional burst frequency.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of model predictions with experimental data.

claim: Dpp and Wg regulation of genes in the wing disc primarily occurs by modulation of transcriptional burst frequency.
source: All of these model predictions agree well with the experimental results (Figure 6C). This suggests that Dpp and Wg regulation of genes in the wing disc primarily occurs by modulation of transcriptional burst frequency.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data and computational modeling.

claim: Transcription of the gene brk is directly regulated by the Dpp effector protein Mothers-against-dpp (Mad).
source: Transcription of the gene brk is directly regulated by the Dpp effector protein Mothers-against-dpp (Mad) (Minami et al., 1999; Moser and Campbell, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mad, in complex with Medea and Schnurri, represses brk transcription.
source: Mad, in complex with Medea and Schnurri, represses brk transcription (Cai and Laughon, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The level of Brk protein is instrumental in repressing the expression of omb and salm, which are induced by Dpp.
source: In turn, the level of Brk protein is instrumental in repressing the expression of omb and salm, which are induced by Dpp (Campbell and Tomlinson, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: omb is less sensitive to Brk repression than salm.
source: Since omb is less sensitive to Brk repression than salm, its expression domain is broader.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about omb and salm regulation.

claim: salm transcription is directly activated by Dpp without participation of Schnurri.
source: salm transcription is directly activated by Dpp without participation of Schnurri (Moser and Campbell, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: omb transcription does not directly depend on Dpp signaling, and its transcriptional activation is brought about by unknown factors.
source: Curiously, omb transcription does not directly depend on Dpp signaling, and its transcriptional activation is brought about by unknown factors (Sivasankaran et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Regulation of transcription burst frequency occurs for omb, brk, and salm despite their diverse molecular mechanisms of regulation.
source: Given the diverse molecular mechanisms by which genes such as omb, brk, and salm are regulated, it is illuminating that regulation of transcription burst frequency occurs for all of them.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: The on-rate, kon, is the most likely rate constant being regulated since it specifically affects burst frequency alone.
source: In the two-state view of promoter kinetics, the on-rate, kon, then is the most likely rate constant being regulated since it specifically affects burst frequency alone (Dar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the two-state model and supported by a citation.

claim: kon determines the average rate at which a promoter will switch from its OFF to its ON state.
source: It determines the average rate at which a promoter will switch from its OFF to its ON state.
evidence: This reflects the definition of kon in the two-state model.

claim: Burst frequency correlates with enhancer strength and enhancer-promoter contact.
source: It has been found that burst frequency correlates with enhancer strength and enhancer-promoter contact, suggesting that kon is potentiated by enhancer-promoter contact and is mediated by transcription factor binding to DNA (Bartman et al., 2016; Bothma et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2019; Fukaya et al., 2016; Larsson et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: kon is potentiated by enhancer-promoter contact and is mediated by transcription factor binding to DNA.
source: It has been found that burst frequency correlates with enhancer strength and enhancer-promoter contact, suggesting that kon is potentiated by enhancer-promoter contact and is mediated by transcription factor binding to DNA (Bartman et al., 2016; Bothma et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2019; Fukaya et al., 2016; Larsson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple cited studies.

claim: Occupancy of Dpp effectors on target enhancers varies the kon rate for their linked promoters.
source: This suggests that occupancy of Dpp effectors on target enhancers varies the kon rate for their linked promoters, and this modulation is negative for repressors such as Brk and positive for activators such as Mad.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings and prior knowledge.

claim: Burst frequency regulation is observed for developmental genes in the embryo.
source: Burst frequency regulation is also observed for developmental genes in the embryo (Bothma et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2019; Fukaya et al., 2016; Garcia et al., 2013; Holloway and Spirov, 2017; Little et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: A common mechanism to regulate patterned gene expression is by control of burst frequency.
source: Thus, a common mechanism to regulate patterned gene expression is by control of burst frequency.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings and prior work.

claim: Burst size can be regulated by cell-cell signaling, as is the case for Notch target genes in the Drosophila embryo.
source: However, burst size can also be regulated by cell-cell signaling, as is the case for Notch target genes in the Drosophila embryo (Falo-Sanjuan et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: eve gene expression in the embryo is regulated by transcription factors that modulate burst frequency, plus there is an orthogonal mechanism that controls the window of time over which a nucleus can transcribe the eve gene.
source: Moreover, eve gene expression in the embryo is regulated by transcription factors that modulate burst frequency, plus there is an orthogonal mechanism that controls the window of time over which a nucleus can transcribe the eve gene (Lammers et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Modeling of various embryonic genes suggests that they transition through several intermediate transcriptionally-silent states before their transcription can begin.
source: Modeling of various embryonic genes suggests that they transition through several intermediate transcriptionally-silent states before their transcription can begin (Desponds et al., 2016; Dufourt et al., 2018; Eck et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Chromatin remodeling factors appear to modulate transitions through intermediate transcriptionally-silent states.
source: Chromatin remodeling factors appear to modulate these transitions (Eck et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A two-state model explains much of the experimental results.
source: Although a two-state model explains much of our experimental results, likely there are other factors that also help determine the expression domains of Dpp-responsive genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: omb and salm mRNA numbers per cell drop gradually with distance from the source of Dpp.
source: Our results challenge the view that salm and omb expression domains have sharp boundaries due to transcription thresholds set by Brk and Dpp. We find that omb and salm mRNA numbers per cell drop gradually with distance from the source of Dpp (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a result based on experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The gradients in omb and salm mRNA number are inversely correlated with the gradient in brk mRNA number.
source: As well, their gradients in mRNA number are inversely correlated with the gradient in brk mRNA number.
evidence: This is an observation based on experimental data.

claim: Salm has relatively constant mRNA number in cells near the AP boundary, and those numbers gradually diminish in cells located more laterally.
source: Salm has relatively constant mRNA number in cells near the AP boundary, and those numbers gradually diminish in cells located more laterally.
evidence: This is an observation based on experimental data.

claim: The domain with constant omb mRNA number is smaller than for salm.
source: A similar pattern is seen with omb, except the domain with constant omb mRNA number is smaller than for salm.
evidence: This is an observation based on experimental data.

claim: The salm and omb enhancer trap reporters as well as anti-Salm immunohistochemistry have reported expression domains with sharp boundaries.
source: However, the salm and omb enhancer trap reporters as well as anti-Salm immunohistochemistry have reported expression domains with sharp boundaries (Mayer et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The discrepancy between mRNA gradients and protein expression domains hints at some threshold of mRNA expression below which protein output drops sharply.
source: Possibly, the discrepancy hints at some threshold of mRNA expression below which protein output drops sharply.
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of the discrepancy.

claim: The previously characterized expression domains for salm and omb may have been distorted by non-linear detection of antibodies.
source: It is also possible that the previously characterized expression domains for salm and omb were distorted by non-linear detection of antibodies that recognize Salm and the protein product of lacZ, β-galactosidase.
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of the discrepancy.

claim: Each wing disc is composed of roughly 50,000 cells organized in a pseudostratified epithelium.
source: Each wing disc is composed of roughly 50,000 cells organized in a pseudostratified epithelium.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1A and reflects established knowledge.

claim: The sfGFP-sens transgenic line rescues the endogenous sens gene based on function and expression.
source: The sfGFP-sens transgenic line was used as described in Cassidy et al., 2013.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Diffraction-limited fluorescent spots captured with a 63X objective at 633 nm wavelength are estimated to be approximately 600 nm in diameter.
source: Diffraction-limited fluorescent spots captured with a 63X objective at 633 nm wavelength are estimated to be approximately 600 nm in diameter (Lipson et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and reflects physical principles of microscopy.

claim: When a cutoff is selected within the plateau, the number of 2D objects identified by threshold segmentation is no more than +/- 5% different than the ground truth.
source: To demonstrate this, we manually curated 347 RNA spots from sub-regions of four independent image stacks, and found that when a cutoff is selected within the plateau, the number of 2D objects identified by threshold segmentation is no more than +/- 5% different than the ground truth.
evidence: This is a validation result based on manual curation of data.

claim: The centroids of identified objects have an average displacement of only two pixels from the manually identified centroids.
source: Furthermore, the centroids of identified objects have an average displacement of only two pixels from the manually identified centroids.
evidence: This is a validation result based on manual curation of data.

claim: Only 7 of 4066 mature RNAs were misidentified as transcription sites.
source: To test the accuracy of this segmentation procedure, we manually inspected three particularly RNA-dense regions in independent images where automated segmentation found a total of 103 transcription sites and 4066 mature RNAs. We determined that only 7 of 4066 mature RNAs were misidentified as transcription sites, and found no examples of transcription sites that had been missed by automated segmentation.
evidence: This is a validation result based on manual inspection of data.

claim: No examples of transcription sites were missed by automated segmentation.
source: To test the accuracy of this segmentation procedure, we manually inspected three particularly RNA-dense regions in independent images where automated segmentation found a total of 103 transcription sites and 4066 mature RNAs. We determined that only 7 of 4066 mature RNAs were misidentified as transcription sites, and found no examples of transcription sites that had been missed by automated segmentation.
evidence: This is a validation result based on manual inspection of data.

claim: The automated method identified at least 85% of nuclei objects identified manually for each image.
source: To ascertain the accuracy of segmentation, we compared results to manually labeled nuclei in four randomly selected disc images. The automated method identified at least 85% of nuclei objects identified manually for each image.
evidence: This is a validation result based on comparison with manual segmentation.

claim: The Voronoi cells do not accurately describe the pseudostratified epithelial nature of wing disc cells.
source: It is important to be clear that the Voronoi cells do not accurately describe the pseudostratified epithelial nature of wing disc cells.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the method.

claim: 3D segmentation of pseudostratified epithelial cells is still something no one working in any system has achieved.
source: However, note that 3D segmentation of pseudostratified epithelial cells is still something no one working in any system has achieved.
evidence: This reflects the current state of the field.

claim: The trends of mRNAs/cell assigned to 100's of cell across the wing disc are trustworthy despite local assignment errors.
source: Clearly we get the transcript assignment incorrect at a local level. However, being the most democratic approach, the trends of mRNAs/cell assigned to 100's of cell across the wing disc are trustworthy.
evidence: This is a justification for the method based on its democratic nature.

claim: Similar trends in RNA and transcription spots feature are observed in each disc individually.
source: Similar trends in RNA and transcription spots feature are observed in each disc individually, and hence, the analysis is not distorted by artifacts in pooling and cell segmentation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The RNA decay parameter kdeg is fixed at 0.04/min for all simulations, as this rate had been experimentally determined for sens mRNA.
source: The RNA decay parameter kdeg is fixed at 0.04/min for all simulations, as this rate had been experimentally determined for sens mRNA (Giri et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.
